title: the Nasadiya Sukta (the hymn of creation — "who really knows?")
hook: rewind the day, then the year, then everything, until there's nothing left to rewind. The hymn of creation starts there, and starts with questions
carry: the Nasadiya Sukta (the hymn of creation — "who really knows?")
tomorrow: the Nasadiya Sukta (the hymn of creation — "who really knows?")

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last look at what the Rig Veda is: a gambler's confession, and Savitar's plain advice, farm your field. Did you catch your own sound of the dice? Day one thousand two hundred fifty.

Run the day backward, like a video on rewind. Dinner un-cooks. The drive home un-drives. Morning coffee pours itself back into the pot. Keep going. Last year unwinds. The house you live in comes apart into lumber, the lumber into trees, the trees into seeds. Keep going, past the first people, past the first mountains, past the first stars. At some point the rewind button has nothing left to rewind. What's there? Or is there even a there? One hymn in the Rig Veda stops at that last frame and stares at it. It's called the Nasadiya Sukta, and today, its first verse.
screen: `RUN THE DAY BACKWARD.` → `PAST THE FIRST STARS.` → `NOTHING LEFT TO REWIND.`

segments.voice: The hymn takes its name from its first words, na asat: not non-being. In paraphrase, it opens like this. Then there was not non-being, and there was not being. There was no air, and no sky beyond it. Stop there for a second. It doesn't say: in the beginning there was nothing. It says even nothing wasn't there yet. Not being, and not non-being either. The usual pair of opposites, is and isn't, hasn't started. No air to breathe, no sky to look up into. And then, instead of an answer, the poet asks questions. What covered it? Where? In whose keeping? Was there water, deep beyond measure? That's the whole first verse. A hymn about creation that begins by refusing to describe it, and asks instead. Some readers hear wonder in that. Some hear a careful thinker, unwilling to claim more than anyone could know. Some Hindu teachers hear a picture of Brahman before names and forms. The hymn itself doesn't say which. It simply puts the questions into the sacred collection, to be chanted. The questions weren't left at the edge of the scripture as doubts. They were kept inside it, and handed down with the rest.
screen: `NA ASAT: NOT NON-BEING.` · `NEITHER BEING NOR NON-BEING.` · `WHAT COVERED IT? WHERE? IN WHOSE CARE?` · `THE QUESTIONS ARE KEPT INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let one question stand. Sit, and let the breath settle. Let a large question come to mind, the hymn's own if you like: what was here before anything? Say it slowly inside. When an answer offers itself, set it down gently, and ask the question again. You don't need to solve it. Keep it the way the hymn keeps its questions, open and cared for. If you pray, you can hold the question in that presence. The bell holds the time.
The Nasadiya Sukta. The Rig Veda's hymn of creation, named from its first words, not non-being, which opens with questions instead of answers. Today's word.

Your line: the Nasadiya Sukta, the hymn of creation, who really knows? Today, when you catch yourself rushing to an answer, ask one more question first, the way the hymn does. Day one thousand two hundred fifty.

howItsDone: The Nasadiya Sukta is chanted as part of the Rig Veda's recited text and is also studied and discussed by Hindu teachers as a reflection on what came before creation.

myth: the hymn's name comes from its first words
Nasadiya, from na asat: not non-being.
the first verse says there was empty nothing
it says there was not non-being, and not being either: even nothing wasn't there yet.
the first verse ends with an answer
it ends with questions: what covered it, where, in whose keeping, was there water?

fork.setup: you're the poet. you've just said there was no being, no non-being, no air, no sky. what do you write next?
options: the name of the god who made it all.
the order in which things were made.
fork.reveal: the first verse turns to questions: what covered it? where? in whose keeping? was there water, deep beyond measure?

original.note: Sanskrit: from na asat, not non-being, the hymn's opening words. Sukta means hymn.

trapdoor: what you thought: the hymn of creation tells how the world was made.
what it means: its first verse refuses to describe the start, and asks questions instead.
what a scholar hears: Rig Veda 10.129.1, nasad asin no sad asit, where being and non-being, sat and asat, are both denied before anything is said.
recall: stilling the movements of the mind
the year just walked and kept
